raw_segments.text: The inhabitants of the United States talk a great deal of their attachment to their
country, but I confess that I do not rely upon that calculating patriotism which is
founded upon interest and which a change in the interests at stake may obliterate.
Nor do I attach much importance to the language of the Americans when they manifest, in their
daily conversations, the intention of maintaining the federal system adopted by their forefathers.
A government retains its sway over a great number of citizens, far less by the voluntary
and rational consent of the multitude than by that instinctive and to a certain extent
involuntary agreement which results from similarity of feelings and resemblances of opinion.
I will never admit that men constitute a social body simply because they obey the same head
Society can only exist when a great number of men consider a great number of things in
the same point of view, when they hold the same opinions upon many subjects, and when
the same occurrences suggest the same thoughts and impressions to their minds.
